newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky says Albanian govt, rebels must talk.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky says Albanian govt, rebels must talk.

text.p: International mediator Franz Vranitzky on Wednesday urged the Albanian government and rebel leaders holding much of the south to start talks to pave the way for elections by June.

Vranitzky, envoy for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), arrived in Albania for his third visit in two months to fierce criticism from supporters of President Sali Berisha over his own contacts with the rebels.

Interior Minister Belul Celo, a member of Berisha's rightist Democratic Party, told Vranitzky that the rebel committees which control much of the south were a "serious obstacle" to the restoration of peace and order.
Vranitzky, who will visit a rebel-held town on Thursday, told reporters that the best way to approach the problem was dialogue between the two sides.
"If there are obstacles in a political system, it doesn't help just to ignore them," he said.
"We think it will be necessary for (rebels and government) to have at least a minimum of dialogue between themselves."

Around a dozen youths stood outside Fino's office where he and ministers were holding talks with the OSCE delegation with banners in Albanian and German reading "Vranitzky, be neutral" and "Don't meet the rebels". Police with guns moved them on.
Vranitzky was due to meet Berisha later on Wednesday.

Rilindja Demokratike, the newspaper of Berisha's party, said Vranitzky's mission may be compromised by the fact that on his last trip in March, he met anti-Berisha rebel leaders but not the president himself.
"Such positions may compromise the neutrality of Vranitzky's mission in Albania and endanger his success -- something we don't want," the paper said.
The pro-Berisha newspaper Albania concurred.
"The minefield he is walking on now might blow up not only his mission but also the future of peace in Albania," it said.
Berisha, under pressure as the Balkan state lurched towards anarchy, last month formed an all-party government led by Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, whose Socialist party was in opposition.
Berisha agreed to early elections by the end of June.
Vranitzky said Fino had said "having elections not later than June...is a must". He added: "I think they are right."

Vranitzky was due to travel early on Thursday with government officials to the rebel-held southern port of Vlore, heart of the insurrection that engulfed Albania at the end of February after the collapse of get-rich-quick investment schemes.
Southerners were among the hardest hit as thousands of people lost their life savings. Rebels have blamed Berisha, a northerner, and say they will not give up until he quits.
Vranitzky will also visit a new troublespot, the government-held northern town of Shkoder, on Thursday.
"I have my duties and I have a mandate and I am definitely not going to let this mandate be curtailed by any newspaper reports," Vranitzky said.
He said it had been useful to listen to the rebels but stressed he would not deal directly with them and did not know whether there would be any contacts during Thursday's trip.
"I see nothing wrong...as long as our main negotiating partner is the government," he said.

Vranitzky, a former Austrian Chancellor, said he was pleased with the start of Operation Alba, an eight-nation security mission to protect humanitarian aid. "I have the feeling that we are on the right track so far," he said.
